predictions.rationale:
Kansas is the more likely winner because the strengths described in these reports line up well against the exact areas Cal Baptist depends on most. CBU’s upset formula is clear: Dominique Daniels Jr. controls late offense, the Lancers generate paint touches and second-chance points, they rebound well, and defensively they shrink the arc while forcing opponents into a physical half-court game. That profile makes them dangerous, especially as a veteran 13-seed with multiple close-game wins. But Kansas brings a version of the same virtues with a higher talent baseline, more size, and stronger defensive ceiling.

The biggest matchup factor is Daniels versus the Kansas defense. CBU’s offense is heavily burdened on Daniels, with low overall assist production and a reliance on individual creation rather than flowing ball movement. The report explicitly notes the downside: if Daniels is contained and the half-court game bogs down, CBU can struggle to manufacture points. Kansas is especially well equipped to test that weakness. Bill Self’s team holds opponents to 38.5% shooting overall and 29.8% from three, with elite back-line protection from Flory Bidunga and additional length from Bryson Tiller. Because Kansas can protect the rim without over-gambling, it is well positioned to force Daniels into the kind of hard twos and late-clock shot attempts that reduce CBU’s efficiency. That matters even more because CBU is not a high-assist team and does not have abundant secondary creation if the first option is disrupted.

Kansas also has a strong answer to one of CBU’s core strengths: rebounding. Cal Baptist’s plus-7.4 rebound margin and committee frontcourt are central to both its offense and defense, especially when it wins with offensive boards and second-chance points. But Kansas is not a fragile rebounding favorite; it averages 38.6 rebounds per game, has Bidunga at 9.2 boards per game, Tre White at 6.8, and Tiller as another active frontcourt presence. CBU may still compete physically, but this is not a matchup where its rebounding edge should automatically carry over the way it can against WAC opponents.

On the other end, Kansas has more diverse scoring options than CBU. Peterson is the premier late-clock shot maker, Council is the main organizer and downhill creator, Bidunga is an efficient interior finisher, White provides secondary scoring and rebounding, and Tiller gives Kansas another frontcourt scorer. By contrast, CBU’s offense is much more top-heavy. If Daniels scores efficiently and Jackson/Williams hit enough shots, the game can stay tight, but Kansas has more ways to get to offense through post feeds, drives, free throws, and offensive balance. That diversity is important against a CBU defense that does a very good job taking away threes and finishing possessions; Kansas does not need to live from deep to score.

CBU’s best case is obvious from the report: make this a slow, physical, close game, keep Kansas out of rhythm, trust Daniels late, and lean on its proven clutch résumé. That path is real, especially because Kansas has had some ugly offensive stretches and has shown vulnerability in losses where the game became messy or where the offense stalled. But even that caveat still favors Kansas slightly, because the Jayhawks also have documented success in close games, including wins over NC State, TCU, Texas Tech, and Arizona, and they bring much more high-major experience and postseason coaching equity with Bill Self.

The reports also point to an important historical clue: CBU was competitive against Colorado but got overwhelmed 91-60 by BYU when facing a high-major size/athlete gap and could not create enough easy offense. Kansas is not described as a dominant juggernaut, but it does have the same kind of size, rim protection, and defensive structure that can recreate that stress. If the Jayhawks keep Daniels out of the paint, contest without fouling too much, and avoid giving up a big offensive-rebound disadvantage, Cal Baptist’s path to enough points becomes narrow.

So while Cal Baptist has genuine upset traits—an elite lead guard, toughness, rebounding, and repeated late-game execution—the specific matchup favors Kansas. The Jayhawks have the personnel to pressure CBU’s one-star-driven offense, enough size to blunt the Lancers’ second-chance game, and more varied scoring options on the other side. The most likely script is a competitive game for stretches, but Kansas gradually controls the paint and wins with defensive resistance and superior frontcourt impact.

Kansas is the safer pick based solely on these reports because its core strengths line up directly against Cal Baptist’s biggest offensive vulnerabilities. Cal Baptist’s offense is heavily dependent on Dominique Daniels Jr. creating late-clock shots, getting to the paint, and carrying a very high usage burden on a team that averages only 10.3 assists per game with a 0.8 assist-turnover ratio. The report explicitly notes that when Daniels is contained and the half-court offense bogs down, CBU can struggle badly, as seen in the 65-46 loss at Utah Valley. That is a dangerous weakness against a Kansas team whose defining trait is elite shot suppression: opponents shoot just 38.5-38.8% from the field and about 29.8% from three, with a 90.3 defensive rating and a profile built on dragging teams into inefficient half-court games. That is exactly the kind of environment most likely to expose Cal Baptist’s low-playmaking, drought-prone offense.

Cal Baptist does have legitimate upset ingredients. Daniels is the best individual late-game scorer in the matchup based on the writeup, the Lancers rebound extremely well with a +7.4 margin, and their defense is strong at running shooters off the line and finishing possessions. They have also repeatedly won close games, including multiple overtime wins and the WAC title comeback over Utah Valley. If the game is tight late, CBU has real evidence that it can execute under pressure. But Kansas is less likely than a typical vulnerable 4-seed to hand over easy chances, because the Jayhawks themselves protect the ball well, with an estimated turnover rate around 13.8%, and play at a controlled 68.5-possession pace that reduces volatility.

The most important matchup factor is that both teams defend the three well, but Kansas has the more reliable underlying offensive floor. CBU shoots only 43.2% from the field and 33.7% from three, while Kansas is at 45.7% overall, 35.1% from three, and 77.2% at the foul line. Kansas is not an overwhelming offense, but it is balanced, takes care of the ball, and has been tested by the nation’s No. 1 NET strength of schedule. Cal Baptist has shown it can beat strong mid-major opponents and compete in stretches against power competition, but the BYU blowout and the Colorado loss suggest the athlete/size gap can become decisive when its offense is forced into difficult twos. Kansas’s defense is specifically built to force those exact shots.

CBU’s rebounding and clutch shot-making give it a path to an upset, especially if Daniels has another takeover game and Kansas’s sometimes-stagnant offense falls into one of its poor shooting stretches. Still, based on the reports, Kansas has more ways to control the game: elite defense, superior schedule-tested resilience, better ball security, solid free-throw shooting, and enough offensive competence to punish a Cal Baptist team that does not generate much easy offense outside Daniels-driven creation. The likely script is a competitive, lower-variance game where Kansas’s defense steadily wears down CBU’s half-court attack and prevents Daniels from getting enough support to finish the upset.

Kansas is the safer pick based on the matchup details in these reports, even though Cal Baptist has several classic upset traits. The case for CBU is real: Dominique Daniels Jr. is exactly the kind of lead guard who can swing a tournament game, CBU rebounds extremely well with a +7.4 margin, and its defense is built to run opponents off the three-point line and finish possessions. CBU also has strong late-game credentials, with multiple one-possession and overtime wins plus the WAC title comeback against Utah Valley. If this game is within a possession in the final minutes, CBU has more proven clutch shot-making than most 13-seeds.

But the stronger overall matchup still leans Kansas because the biggest structural weakness in Cal Baptist’s profile lines up poorly against Kansas’s biggest strength. CBU’s offense is heavily dependent on Daniels creating difficult shots in a low-assist, low-flow system; they average only 10.3 assists per game with a 0.8 assist-turnover ratio, and the report explicitly notes offensive drought risk when Daniels is forced into hard twos without foul-line relief. Kansas is a defense-first team allowing just 68.8 points per game, with high-end size and rim protection anchored by Flory Bidunga, who brings 14.9 points, 9.2 rebounds, and 2.2 blocks-level production. Against a team like CBU that prefers paint pressure, second chances, and individual creation over ball movement, Kansas has the personnel to crowd Daniels, challenge at the rim, and make secondary creators beat them.

CBU’s defense is disciplined and should help keep Kansas from getting easy rhythm threes, and the Kansas analysis makes clear that the Jayhawks become vulnerable when opponents erase transition and force half-court execution. That is the main reason this projects as competitive rather than comfortable. CBU’s conservative style, strong rebounding, and ability to shrink the arc could absolutely drag Kansas into the kind of lower-possession game that has caused problems for the Jayhawks in losses to Iowa State, Arizona State, Houston, and others. However, there is an important difference between those teams and Cal Baptist: those opponents brought high-major physicality, depth, and multiple disruptive athletes. The CBU report itself includes warning signs against that caliber of team, especially the 91-60 loss to BYU and the note that CBU can struggle when the athlete/size gap rises and the offense cannot generate enough easy twos. Kansas presents a similar kind of problem, especially with Bidunga inside, Tre White on the wing, and Darryn Peterson as the best perimeter scorer in the game outside Daniels.

Kansas also has more offensive paths to a workable number. Even if Cal Baptist succeeds in reducing transition, Kansas can still lean on Peterson’s 19.5 points per game, White’s 14.0 and rebounding, and Bidunga’s interior efficiency. CBU, by contrast, is much more top-heavy. Daniels is elite, Williams is useful as a second option, and Jackson can provide spacing, but the offense is not built on consistent shared creation. If Kansas can contain Daniels even moderately, CBU may not have enough playmaking diversity to sustain scoring for 40 minutes.

The game script most favorable to CBU is obvious: defensive rebounding, no live-ball turnovers, Daniels controlling tempo, and a late close game. But based solely on these reports, Kansas is more likely to win because it has the superior defensive ceiling, the better size/athletic profile, more reliable interior presence, and enough scoring options to survive an ugly half-court game. Cal Baptist has upset potential, but Kansas is the more complete team and the likelier winner unless Daniels delivers another extraordinary shot-making performance.

Kansas is the stronger pick based on the interaction between these two profiles. Cal Baptist’s report describes a solid top-100ish mid-major whose résumé is better than its predictive quality: NET 98, Torvik 96, KenPom 106, and BPI 137, with a very soft schedule and almost no high-end win equity. The Lancers went 18-0 in Quadrant 4 and were reliable against weak opposition, but they were only 0-1 in Quadrant 1 and 2-4 in Quadrant 2, which suggests limited proof that their style scales against top-40 caliber teams. Kansas, by contrast, has repeatedly beaten elite opponents—Tennessee, Baylor, Iowa State, Arizona, Houston, Texas Tech—and did so with a profile built on defense, paint control, and high-major size, all of which are especially relevant against Cal Baptist’s weaknesses.

The biggest matchup issue for Cal Baptist is offense. Their analysis points to a low-assist, low-scoring, somewhat three-point-dependent attack that can bog down badly when jumpers are not falling. ESPN lists them at just 72.8 points per game with only 10.4 assists per game, and the report explicitly notes limited half-court creation, modest free-throw generation, and offensive volatility tied to shooting variance. That is a dangerous formula against a Kansas defense that held opponents to 38.5% shooting overall and 29.8% from three, with elite rim protection from Flory Bidunga and additional length from Bryson Tiller. If Cal Baptist is already not a strong foul-drawing team and tends to rely on perimeter shotmaking, Kansas’s shell defense, disciplined closeouts, and back-line shot blocking directly attack the Lancers’ offensive path to an upset.

Cal Baptist’s strengths—defense, rebounding, and comfort in ugly games—do give them a theoretical chance to keep the score down and compress variance. Their defensive glass appears strong, and the report is clear that they are more dangerous in a slow, low-efficiency game than in a track meet. But Kansas is also comfortable in that exact kind of game. The Jayhawks are described as more trustworthy defensively than offensively, with a Bill Self identity built on defending, owning the glass, and getting paint touches. This means Cal Baptist is unlikely to drag Kansas into an unfamiliar style. In fact, an ugly half-court game probably still favors Kansas because the Jayhawks have the better interior scoring options, the better rim protection, and the better individual shot creators in Darryn Peterson and Melvin Council Jr.

That shot-creation gap is probably decisive. Cal Baptist’s report emphasizes that their offense can stagnate and that they do not appear to have top-end creators capable of consistently generating efficient offense against top defenses. Kansas, even when not aesthetically smooth, has multiple proven answers: Peterson as the primary late-clock scorer and mismatch hunter, Council as a downhill playmaker, Bidunga as a high-efficiency interior finisher, plus White and Tiller as secondary options. Kansas has already shown it can win close, physical games and has a 5-1 record in tight games cited in the report. Cal Baptist may defend well enough to keep Kansas from exploding offensively, but the Lancers’ own scoring ceiling looks too low to count on fourty-minute upset offense against this level of defense.

The rebounding battle is the one area where Cal Baptist could compete, since they are strong on the glass and that can help stabilize a poor shooting night. But Kansas is also a strong rebounding and paint team, and unlike many major-conference teams, it does not rely solely on finesse or spacing. The Jayhawks’ frontcourt size and physicality should prevent Cal Baptist from turning rebounding into a major edge. And on the other end, Kansas’s ability to generate free throws, post touches, and interior finishes is a bad sign for a Cal Baptist team whose profile suggests it survives by flattening weaker opponents rather than overwhelming strong ones.

Overall, the reports point to Cal Baptist as disciplined and credible, but not especially well equipped to exploit Kansas’s flaws. Kansas has the superior schedule-tested résumé, the more proven defense, the much better shot creation, and a front line that should punish Cal Baptist’s limited offensive versatility. If the game is slow and ugly, Cal Baptist can hang around for stretches, but Kansas is still more likely to control the paint, create the better late-clock looks, and separate over the final ten minutes.

Kansas should be favored based on the gap in team quality, schedule-tested performance, and the specific way these profiles interact. The Jayhawks rate far higher in every major predictive system cited: NET 21 versus 98 for Cal Baptist, KenPom 21 versus 106, BPI 22 versus 137, and Torvik 22 versus 96. Just as important, Kansas built that profile against the nation’s No. 1 NET strength of schedule, while Cal Baptist’s schedule was very soft, with a NET SOS of 215 and non-conference NET SOS of 274. Cal Baptist’s 25-8 record is respectable, but the reports make clear that it was driven more by handling weaker opponents than by proving itself against top competition; the Lancers were 0-1 in Quad 1 and 2-4 in Quad 2, with most of their value coming from avoiding bad losses and going 18-0 in Quad 4. That makes this a major class jump.

The matchup itself also leans Kansas. Cal Baptist’s biggest offensive concerns are low assist volume, modest scoring output, inconsistent half-court creation, and apparent dependence on jump shooting and three-point variance. ESPN lists the Lancers at only 72.8 points per game with just 10.4 assists per game, and the analysis notes that when they are not making threes, their offense can bog down badly. That is a dangerous weakness against a Kansas defense that is the clear backbone of its team profile. Kansas allows opponents to shoot only 38.5% from the field and 29.8% from three, with an elite 90.3 defensive rating and strong overall shot suppression. In simple terms, the exact thing Cal Baptist most needs offensively—enough perimeter shotmaking to compensate for limited foul drawing and creation—is the exact thing Kansas is best equipped to take away.

Cal Baptist’s path would be to make this ugly, slow, and rebound-driven, and there is some evidence they can do that. The Lancers defend well enough to stay competitive, rebound the defensive glass effectively, and have recent form suggesting they can win even with poor shooting. Kansas is also not an overwhelming offense; it is described as solid but not dominant, and its late-season losses show that the offense can bog down. So the underdog case is real: if Cal Baptist turns the game into a low-possession grinder, protects the glass, and gets hot from three, Kansas is not explosive enough to guarantee instant separation.

But even granting that, Kansas still has the stronger underlying edge. The Jayhawks are not just better defensively; they are also cleaner offensively, with a very low turnover rate, balanced shot profile, solid offensive rebounding, and strong free-throw shooting at 77.2%. That matters in a tournament-style game where empty possessions and late-game execution are decisive. Cal Baptist’s offense appears more fragile and more sensitive to shooting variance, while Kansas’s defense is more bankable. And although Kansas is not an elite offensive machine, it has faced and survived a much tougher slate, going 9-9 in Quad 1 and 7-1 in Quad 2. Compared with Cal Baptist’s résumé, that suggests Kansas is far more prepared for this caliber of opponent than Cal Baptist is for Kansas’s level of athleticism and defensive structure.

Overall, Cal Baptist’s strengths—defense, rebounding, comfort in ugly games—could keep the margin respectable for stretches. But based solely on these reports, Kansas has too much advantage in proven quality, defensive matchup fit, and schedule-adjusted reliability. The most likely outcome is that Kansas’s elite defense squeezes Cal Baptist’s already-limited offense, while its steadier offensive floor produces enough points to control the game.

Kansas is the more likely winner because the matchup report describes a team with clearly superior top-end talent, stronger defense against quality competition, and more ways to control the game than Cal Baptist’s profile suggests. Cal Baptist’s overall résumé is respectable at 25-8, but the underlying indicators are modest: NET 98, KenPom 106, Torvik 96, and BPI 137, with a very weak strength of schedule and almost no high-end wins (0-1 Q1, 2-4 Q2, 18-0 Q4). That matters here because the Lancers’ profile is built more on consistently beating weaker teams than on proving they can score efficiently against power-conference size and athleticism.

The biggest separator is offensive ceiling and shot creation. Cal Baptist’s analysis points to a defense-first team with a limited half-court offense: only 72.8 points per game, an extremely low 10.4 assists per game, poor national scoring rank, inconsistent efficiency, and evidence of three-point dependence without reliable foul drawing. The report explicitly says their offense can bog down badly when jumpers are not falling. That is a dangerous flaw against a Kansas team whose best trait is still defense. Kansas allows just 68.8 points per game, was holding opponents to 36.6% shooting and 25.2% from three before league play, and has real interior disruption with Flory Bidunga’s rim protection and rebounding. A team like Cal Baptist that already struggles to create easy offense and does not generate many assisted or rim-pressure baskets is exactly the kind of opponent Kansas is built to suffocate.

Cal Baptist’s best path would be to make the game ugly, slow, and half-court oriented, because Kansas is vulnerable when transition is removed and it has to execute late in the shot clock. The Kansas report is very clear on that: Iowa State, Arizona State, UCF, Arizona, and Houston all caused offensive problems by cutting off early offense, changing coverages, and forcing Kansas into stagnant possessions. But Cal Baptist is not described as a pressure team that creates lots of turnovers or as an offense capable of consistently punishing Kansas once the game slows down. The Lancers rebound well and defend well enough to keep scores manageable, but their own offense is even less trustworthy than Kansas’s. So while they may succeed in dragging Kansas into a lower-possession game, that does not automatically favor them if they cannot get to the mid-to-high 60s efficiently.

Kansas also has matchup advantages at the top of the roster that Cal Baptist’s report does not really answer. Darryn Peterson is the highest-level perimeter scorer in the game at 19.5 points per game, Tre White adds 14.0 points and 6.8 rebounds as a physical wing stabilizer, and Bidunga gives Kansas an interior force at 14.9 points on elite finishing plus rebounding and shot blocking. Cal Baptist’s report emphasizes defensive rebounding and discipline, but it does not present evidence of high-end rim protection, dynamic perimeter creation, or the kind of offensive versatility needed to attack Kansas’s weaker spots. If Kansas can get anything close to normal production from Peterson and White, Cal Baptist may struggle to match it possession for possession.

Another reason to lean Kansas is that Cal Baptist’s upset formula relies heavily on shooting variance. The Lancers’ offense appears to rise and fall with eFG% and three-point accuracy, while their free-throw generation is limited and assist rate is poor. Kansas’s losses come when opponents force its offense into inefficiency, but Cal Baptist’s own profile suggests exactly the same vulnerability, only more severe. In a slow, defensive game, the team with better individual creators and higher-caliber athletes usually has the edge, and the reports strongly indicate that is Kansas.

Finally, coaching and competition level favor Kansas. Bill Self’s team has shown bounce-back ability and adjustment strength, and even Kansas’s bad offensive performances came against strong, athletic major-conference defenses. Cal Baptist, by contrast, built its record against a soft schedule and lacks evidence of success versus teams with Kansas’s combination of size, rebounding, rim pressure, and defensive talent. The most likely outcome is that Cal Baptist keeps the game competitive for stretches by defending and rebounding, but Kansas’s superior talent, interior edge, and ability to generate enough offense through Peterson, White, and Bidunga carry the day. The game script most supported by the reports is a relatively low-scoring Kansas win rather than a Cal Baptist upset.

Kansas is the safer and more likely winner because the Jayhawks’ core strengths line up directly against the specific pressure points in Cal Baptist’s profile. Cal Baptist is heavily dependent on Dominique Daniels Jr. as a 5-foot-10, high-usage, on-ball creator in a low-assist, half-court offense. The report repeatedly shows that when opponents load up on Daniels, shrink driving lanes, and force the rest of the Lancers to create, Cal Baptist’s efficiency falls sharply. Utah Valley and UT Arlington provided the clearest examples: Daniels either struggled badly on volume shooting or scored without enough support, while team turnovers spiked and overall offense stalled. That is a dangerous setup against a Kansas defense built on point-of-attack discipline, hard help, and elite rim protection from Flory Bidunga and Bryson Tiller. Kansas does not need to gamble wildly to disrupt CBU; its normal shell principles already fit the blueprint Cal Baptist dislikes most.

The size and athleticism gap also favors Kansas in the exact places that matter. Cal Baptist has frontcourt height, but the analysis says those bigs are more rebounders and finishers than self-creators, and they can be exposed by high-major athleticism. Kansas brings not just size but functional size: Bidunga is a high-level finisher and shot blocker, Tiller adds mobility and rim protection, and Tre White contributes rebounding and physicality from the wing. That means Kansas is better equipped than most opponents to contest Daniels at the point of attack, rotate behind the play, and still control the glass. Cal Baptist’s usual advantage of being big for a mid-major is muted here because Kansas can match or exceed it while also being more dynamic offensively.

Tempo and possession style are another major factor. Cal Baptist is most comfortable in lower-possession grind games, but Kansas has shown it can win that kind of game while also having far more offensive ceiling. The Jayhawks beat strong teams like Houston, Iowa State, Baylor, and Arizona with defense-first basketball and half-court execution, so even if Cal Baptist succeeds in slowing the pace, Kansas is still operating in a familiar environment. Conversely, if Kansas can speed the game even modestly through defensive rebounding, early offense, or turnover creation from ball pressure, that pushes Cal Baptist away from its comfort zone. The Lancers’ losses in turnover-heavy games are especially relevant because their ballhandling beyond Daniels appears fragile, while Kansas has the length and physicality to make entries, drives, and second-side decisions difficult.

Offensively, Kansas has multiple answers while Cal Baptist appears to have one primary engine. Darryn Peterson gives Kansas a late-clock shot maker and perimeter mismatch hunter, Melvin Council Jr. supplies playmaking and downhill creation, Bidunga gives them interior finishing and offensive rebounding, and White and Tiller provide secondary scoring and glue play. That diversity matters against a Cal Baptist defense that is solid enough to survive slow games but has been vulnerable when facing high-major athleticism and when forced to defend in space. The reports note that teams can attack Daniels’ size with bigger guards, and Kansas is well positioned to do that with Peterson and Council. Even if Cal Baptist loads up to make Kansas earn it in the half court, the Jayhawks have several credible scoring sources; Cal Baptist does not.

Coaching and tournament context also tilt toward Kansas. Rick Croy’s staff deserves credit for adjustment ability, especially in rematches, but Bill Self’s résumé, tactical flexibility, and history of surviving first-weekend games remain a substantial edge. Kansas may not be dominant enough to make this automatic, and its own offense has shown periods of stagnation in losses to UConn, Iowa State, Cincinnati, Arizona, and Arizona State. But Cal Baptist’s best upset path requires Daniels to both score efficiently against length and avoid the turnover traps that have derailed this team before, while also getting enough secondary creation from a roster that has not consistently shown it. Based on the matchup data provided, Kansas is the team more likely to control the paint, limit Daniels’ downhill game, exploit size mismatches offensively, and win a game that should increasingly favor the higher-level roster as it unfolds.

Kansas is the stronger pick because the specific things Cal Baptist depends on most line up poorly against the specific things Kansas does best. Cal Baptist’s offense is heavily centered on Dominique Daniels Jr., a 5-foot-10, ultra-high-usage guard who drives the offense through on-ball creation, foul drawing, and self-created scoring. The report makes clear that CBU is not a high-assist, equal-opportunity offense; it is creator-centric, with Daniels taking an enormous share of the shots and the supporting cast functioning more as complementary finishers and spot-up options. The same report also identifies the defensive blueprint against CBU: physical point-of-attack defense, early help, shrinking driving lanes, and forcing Daniels into a high-volume, lower-efficiency game while making secondary players create. That blueprint aligns almost perfectly with Kansas’s identity. Kansas is described as a defense-first team with elite shot suppression, allowing just 38.5% from the field and 29.8% from three, with a 90.3 defensive rating and a top-tier national standing in field-goal percentage defense. Against a Cal Baptist team that already struggles when Daniels is pressured and when turnovers rise, Kansas’s defensive profile is an especially dangerous matchup.

The turnover issue is another major reason to favor Kansas. Cal Baptist’s analysis repeatedly points to ball-pressure vulnerability rather than any proven zone weakness. In their worst losses, turnovers spiked badly: 23 and 20 against Utah Valley, 17 against UT Arlington, and those games coincided with major offensive drop-offs. CBU can survive ugly shotmaking nights if it protects the ball, as it did in the WAC title game, but Kansas’s controlled, disciplined style and defensive strength suggest the Jayhawks are well equipped to keep Cal Baptist from playing comfortably. Even though Kansas is not described as a frantic pace team, it does not need to be. Its half-court defense alone is a problem for a team so dependent on one undersized creator and so limited in secondary playmaking.

Kansas also matches up well with Cal Baptist’s preferred tempo. CBU is most comfortable in slower, grind-out games, but Kansas is also comfortable in controlled possessions. The difference is that Kansas has proven it can win those games against the nation’s hardest schedule, while Cal Baptist’s low-possession formula becomes fragile when Daniels is contained. The reports suggest Kansas wins with sturdy half-court defense, low offensive turnover rate, and enough offensive competence to survive without explosive scoring. That is a strong tournament formula against a mid-major whose offense is narrow in construction. Cal Baptist’s size in the frontcourt is real, but the analysis emphasizes that those bigs are more rebounders and finishers than polished interior creators. Kansas’s defense should be able to focus on Daniels without being overly punished by CBU’s frontcourt as a self-sustaining scoring threat.

Cal Baptist does have some paths to competitiveness. Daniels is talented enough to keep them afloat, the team rebounds well, and coach Rick Croy has shown adjustment ability in rematches. Kansas is also not an overwhelming offensive machine; the Jayhawks can bog down offensively and are described as dangerous but imperfect, with some ugly losses when shotmaking disappears. So this is not a prediction that Kansas will automatically blow CBU out. But based solely on the reports, the matchup still favors Kansas because Cal Baptist’s main weakness—dependence on one small, high-usage guard and vulnerability to pressure and disrupted possession flow—runs directly into Kansas’s clearest strength, which is elite-level defense and shot suppression. Kansas’s higher floor, stronger résumé, and more reliable defensive identity make the Jayhawks the more likely winner.

Kansas is the more likely winner because the matchup described in the reports lines up with several of Cal Baptist’s clearest pressure points. Cal Baptist is heavily dependent on Dominique Daniels Jr. as a high-usage, on-ball creator in a guard-driven half-court offense, and the report repeatedly says the best way to beat the Lancers is with physical point-of-attack defense, early help, and schemes that force secondary players to create. That is exactly the kind of profile Kansas is best equipped to attack. Kansas is characterized as a defense-first team that rebounds, protects the rim, and has size and length across the floor, with Flory Bidunga anchoring the interior and wings like Tre White plus bigger guards around him. Against a Cal Baptist team whose offense can bog down when Daniels is forced into volume scoring and whose assist numbers suggest limited shared creation, Kansas has the personnel to crowd Daniels, shrink driving lanes, and challenge the rest of the roster to beat them. The Cal Baptist report specifically notes Daniels is only 5-foot-10 and that long guards can bother him; Kansas is one of the few teams in this matchup with the defensive size to make that matter on every possession.

The turnover angle is especially important. The Cal Baptist analysis identifies ball pressure as a major weakness, with losses featuring 17, 20, and 23 turnovers and major offensive collapses against Utah Valley and UT Arlington. Kansas is not described as a constant full-court pressure team, but it is a defense-first group that thrives on rebounds, blocks, live-ball stops, and turning defense into easier offense. Even if Kansas does not play fast in raw tempo terms, the Jayhawks do their best work when they can generate efficient transition chances off exactly the kinds of mistakes Cal Baptist has shown it can make under pressure. If Kansas can push Daniels into a difficult shot diet while also forcing CBU’s secondary handlers into rushed decisions, the possession battle should tilt toward the Jayhawks.

Kansas also has the more reliable frontcourt mismatch. Cal Baptist has height, but its own report makes clear that its bigs are more rebounders and finishers than polished offensive creators, and that high-major athleticism has exposed this. Kansas, by contrast, has a true interior problem in Bidunga, who is identified as a rim-pressure, offensive-rebounding, shot-blocking centerpiece. That matters because Cal Baptist prefers slower, grind-out games and leans on its size to rebound and keep games controlled. Kansas is strong enough on the glass and explosive enough around the rim to neutralize some of that comfort. Offensively, Kansas can attack CBU’s undersized lead guard and make the Lancers defend bigger, stronger creators and rollers. Defensively, Kansas can live with help toward Daniels because Cal Baptist’s supporting cast is described as complementary rather than dynamic.

Cal Baptist’s best path would be to drag Kansas into a stagnant half-court game, limit transition, protect the ball, and hope Daniels can win late-clock possessions. The Kansas report does acknowledge that the Jayhawks can become vulnerable when opponents erase transition and force them into low-efficiency half-court offense, as shown by games against Iowa State, Arizona State, Arizona, and Houston. But Cal Baptist’s profile does not look ideally built to exploit that weakness at the highest level. The Lancers are themselves more comfortable in lower-possession games, but their offense is even more creator-dependent and less assist-driven than Kansas’s. Kansas may have half-court scoring drought risk, but Cal Baptist has both that risk and a more severe dependence on one small guard against a long, physical defense. In a game where both teams are comfortable enough in the half court, Kansas still has the better individual talent, rim protection, interior scoring, and defensive tools.

The most decisive matchup factor from the reports is that the exact blueprint for stopping Cal Baptist overlaps with Kansas’s identity better than Cal Baptist’s blueprint for stopping Kansas overlaps with CBU’s identity. To beat Cal Baptist, the report says to load up on Daniels with length, pressure the guards, and force second-side decisions.
